1.explanation: The file src/languages/ruby.js is responsible for defining Ruby’s tokenization rules, including the syntax for character literals (the “?” notation). The regular expressions in this file currently only cover the simplest cases (printable ASCII letters, basic escapes) and do not include patterns for slash, escaped backslash, non-ASCII, Unicode codepoint braces, or control/meta sequences. To fix the bug, you must update the literal/regex definitions in ruby.js so that these additional forms are recognized and highlighted as character literals rather than mistaken for regex or invalid syntax.
1.bug_scenario: When using Ruby’s single‐character literal syntax (the “?” prefix), only the simplest cases (like “?a”) are highlighted correctly. More complex forms – including “?/” (the slash itself), escaped backslashes (“?\\”), non-ASCII characters (“?あ”), Unicode codepoint notation (“?\u{1AF9}”), and control/meta combinations (“?\C-a”, “?\M-a”, etc.) – currently either break highlighting or are treated as the start of a regex rather than a character literal. In the screenshots the valid literals parse as strings, but “?/” becomes a regex token and the other forms aren’t recognized at all. The expected behavior is that all of these “?”‐prefixed character literals are highlighted consistently as string literals.

2.explanation: All of Ruby’s syntax rules live in ruby.js under src/languages.  That file defines the regexes and modes for string, regex and character literal parsing.  Its current character-literal pattern only handles the simplest form (`?.`), so sequences like `?/`, escaped backslashes, Unicode escapes and control/meta prefixes fall through (and in the case of `?/`, get mistaken for a regex).  To fix the bug, ruby.js must be updated with expanded rules covering these unsupported ?x notations.
2.bug_scenario: When highlighting Ruby source code, the built-in grammar misparses many of Ruby’s “?x” character literal forms.  Simple cases like `?a` work, but `?/` is treated as the start of a regex, escapes like `?\\` and unicode forms like `?\u{1234}`, non-ASCII (`?あ`), control/meta (`?\C-a`, `?\M-\C-x`) and other variants aren’t recognized, leading to incorrect tokenization and broken highlighting (see screenshots above).
